newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sugar beet output to slip but reserves high.
newsitem.headline: Russia sugar beet output to slip but reserves high.

text.p: Russia's sugar beet harvest is likely to be one of the worst in decades, but industry analysts said on Monday that high reserves of whites and cheap Ukrainian imports would compensate for low output.
"We still expect the beet harvest to total 17 million tonnes," Mikhail Sushkov, head of the Rossakhsvyokla sugar beet producers' association, said.
Last year's sugar beet harvest was officially a low 19.1 million tonnes, far below the average 33.2 million tonnes seen each year over 1986-1990.
Independent agricultural analyst Andrei Sizov of SovEcon Ltd said the 1996 crop would be 16-17 million tonnes, the second-worst in 40 years.
"Refined sugar reserves are still very high, so despite the low harvest, there will no be increased demand for imports," he said.
He said the 1996 sugar beet crop would likely produce 1.6-1.7 million tonnes of refined white sugar, down from 2.06 million tonnes in 1995.

"Recent numbers show Russia will produce 150,000-200,000 tonnes less refined sugar than it did last year," said one Western trader. "But the decrease is not much compared to consumption, which is 4.6-5.0 million tonnes per year."
He said that imports of non-Ukrainian sugar would find it tough to compete with Ukrainian material to fill in the gaps.

Ukrainian imports are subject to a 10 percent value-added tax from October 1, but traders have said Ukrainian producers have room to mark down their prices before exporting and that they would continue deliveries to Russia at steady levels for at least the next six months.
Ukraine is expected to produce 2.8-3.0 million tonnes of refined sugar in 1996, down from 3.49 in 1995, and to export about one million tonnes to Russia.
"Taxes are a real barrier to the import of refined sugar, except for sugar from Ukraine," the trader said.
Industry sources said the Russian beet harvest, which is only beginning, could still be affected by bad weather.

Sushkov said rain had slowed work at the beginning of the harvest. "It rained all last week and the harvest stopped, but the rain has already ended and the harvest will begin again," he said, adding that dry weather earlier had stifled growth.
Sizov said beet-gathering was proceeding slowly, with 864,000 tonnes harvested by September 16, and that beet quality was threatened.
"Earlier estimates (that output could be higher) were based on the sown area, but now we can look at the early harvest and a few figures show that yields are lower than last year," he said.

Yields in the Northern Caucasus, the first region to be harvested, were 21.9 tonnes per hectare, versus 22.9 tonnes in 1995. In the Central Black Earth (Central-Chernozem) area, yields fell to 16.0 tonnes per hectare from 19.1 tonnes in 1995.
"The harvest is slower because of the weather," Sizov said. "And beets that sit in the ground too long lose sugar content."
